title: Capability bloat in agent tool configurations
titleVi: Tình trạng dư thừa năng lực trong cấu hình công cụ của tác tử

units.text: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
What you will be able to do
Explain what an oversized tool set costs an agent in context, attention and tool-selection accuracy
Read an agent configuration and find overlapping, unused or vaguely described tools and MCP servers the agent doesn't need
Merge overlapping tools into higher-level ones and namespace the remaining tools by service and resource
Limit each agent and subagent to the tools its role needs using tools, disallowedTools, mcpServers and permission modes
Pick between consolidation, scoping, tool search, prompt caching and context editing based on where the context pressure comes from
Key concept
Capability bloat

Capability bloat is when an agent is given more tools than its job needs: tools that overlap, sit unused, have vague descriptions, or come in from MCP servers it never calls. Every one of those definitions takes up context and is one more option Claude has to rule out, so the agent becomes less accurate at choosing a tool, not more capable.
In this lesson

What too many tools cost an agent

Every tool definition you attach is paid for in context before the agent reads the user's request. Claude sees each tool's name, description and input schema on every turn. Fifty tools can use 10–20K tokens. A typical multi-server setup that connects GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana and Splunk can use about 55k tokens on definitions before Claude has done any work. Those tokens come out of the same window the task needs for files, tool results and reasoning.

The cost goes beyond space. Context behaves like an attention budget, and every added token draws it down. As the token count rises, the model gets worse at recalling and reasoning over what's in the window. A tool catalogue the agent mostly ignores still takes attention on every request. In a long-running agent, those definitions compete with the growing pile of
blocks, and the agent can run out of context before it finishes the task.
Predict first
A team adds another 25 MCP tools to an agent that already has 30, on the theory that more capability means more tasks get solved. What is the most likely effect on tool use?
Tool selection gets less accurate, because the agent now has to choose among more than 30–50 loaded tools
No change in accuracy, because Claude ignores tools that aren't relevant to the request
Accuracy improves, because Claude has a better-fitting tool for more requests

The third cost is wrong choices. Claude picks the right tool less reliably once more than roughly 30–50 tools are loaded at the same time. Overlap makes this worse at any size: if two tools both look like they could answer a request, Claude can pick the wrong one, call the right one with the wrong parameters, or spend turns on a roundabout strategy. A wrong tool call costs a round trip, adds a misleading result to the history, and sometimes performs an action nobody wanted. That last case is why bloat matters for safety as well as cost.
Checkpoint 1 of 8
Check yourself

A long-running support agent has GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana and Splunk MCP servers attached. On short requests it works well. On long multi-step investigations it often runs out of context before it finishes. What is the most likely reason the toolset contributes to this?
The toolset only matters if Claude calls the wrong tool; tools it never calls take up no context
The definitions cost tokens, but the context limit applies only to the user's messages and the model's reasoning, not to tools
It doesn't contribute: tool definitions are sent only on the first turn, so only the tool results fill the window later
The tool definitions sit in context on every turn and share the same window as the growing pile of tool_result blocks, leaving less room for the task

Diagnosing bloat in a configuration
A bloat review reads the configuration against the agent's real workflow and asks one question of every entry: what would break if this were gone? Four kinds of finding come up again and again.
Overlapping tools.
Two or more tools do much the same job, such as
and
, or separate get-by-id and list endpoints that are always called together.
Unused tools.
Definitions the agent never calls in its actual tasks. These are often whole MCP servers connected "just in case".
Vague descriptions.
A tool whose purpose Claude can't tell apart from a neighbour's, or whose parameters it keeps getting wrong.
Over-connected MCP servers.
Servers picked up from project files, user settings, plugins or organisation connectors that this agent never meant to use.

Transcripts and metrics are better evidence than reading the config. Record the total number of tool calls, token consumption and tool errors per task, and read the raw tool calls rather than only the agent's own account of what it did. The patterns that show up point to specific fixes. A run of tool errors for invalid parameters usually means a description needs to be clearer or needs examples. Tools that are always called in the same order are candidates for merging. Tools that never appear in any transcript are candidates for removal.

Consolidating and namespacing tools

Consolidation fixes overlap by building tools around tasks rather than endpoints. A common mistake is to write tools that simply wrap existing software functions or API endpoints one-to-one. The agent then has to chain them, reading every intermediate result into its context. A single tool can do several discrete operations or API calls internally and return only what the task needs.
Endpoint-shaped tools merged into task-shaped ones
Instead of
Implement
What the agent no longer has to do
list_users, list_events, create_event
schedule_event
Find availability itself across three calls
read_logs
search_logs
Read entire logs to find the relevant lines
get_customer_by_id, list_transactions, list_notes
get_customer_context
Put a customer's recent history together from three results
list_contacts
search_contacts or message_contact
Scan every contact token by token

Consolidating pays off twice. There are fewer definitions in context, which keeps the agent further below the 30–50-tool range where selection starts to degrade. And work that used to be the agent's reasoning moves into the tool, so the agent has fewer chances to make a mistake. Give each surviving tool one clear purpose that differs from its neighbours. Tool boundaries should split work the way a person with the same resources would split it.
Namespacing deals with the tools that rightly remain. When an agent can reach many servers, put related tools under shared prefixes: by service (
) and, within a service, by resource (

). Claude can then tell two search tools apart before it reads either description. Some MCP clients add prefixes by default. Whether the prefix goes at the start or the end of the name has had measurable effects on tool-use evaluations, and the effect differs between models. Choose the scheme by running your own evaluation, not by habit.
Apply it to your own work
Pick an agent you've built or reviewed. Which two of its tools are almost always called one after the other, and what would a single task-shaped tool replacing them be called?
Checkpoint 3 of 8
Check yourself

Your team is adding namespaces to an agent's tools across Asana and Jira. One engineer wants service prefixes such as asana_projects_search. Another wants suffixes such as projects_search_asana. How should the team decide?
Run the team's own tool-use evaluations on both schemes with the model the agent uses, because the effect differs between models
Use suffixes, because Claude reads the action word first and that always gives more accurate tool selection
Pick either one, because Claude only reads the descriptions, so where the namespace goes has no measurable effect
Use prefixes, because some MCP clients add prefixes by default and that makes prefixes the correct scheme

Scoping tools to each agent's role
Scoping gives each agent or subagent only the tools its role needs. In the Agent SDK this is the subagent's
field, set in its own
. A subagent doesn't automatically get a narrower set than its parent: if you leave
out, it inherits every tool available to subagents. A code reviewer launched by a lead agent that has
and
therefore gets all three unless its own definition lists something narrower. Notes in CLAUDE.md and the parent's permission mode don't change the reviewer's tool set.
A read-only reviewer subagent: its own tools field limits it to read and search, whatever tools the parent has

Removal works at server level too.

Predict first
A headless CI agent is configured with allowedTools: ["Read", "Glob", "Grep"] and no other settings. Claude decides to call Bash. What happens?
Bash runs, because allowedTools only applies to file tools
Bash isn't pre-approved, so the call falls through to the permission mode and the canUseTool callback
Bash is unavailable, because allowedTools is the agent's complete tool list
Approving a tool and scoping a tool are separate controls.
approves tools in advance so they run without a prompt, but it doesn't stop Claude from calling other tools. The permission mode decides what happens to those other calls. In
, any call that needs approval and matches no allow rule goes to your
callback, which is no use in a CI job with nobody to answer. In
, any call that would have prompted is denied, and
is never called. An allowlist combined with
is the closed configuration a headless agent needs: listed tools run and everything else is refused.
A closed, non-interactive tool surface: three tools pre-approved, every other tool call denied
javascript
The other modes go the opposite way.
lets tools run without prompts, apart from the few actions no mode auto-approves. Combined with a denylist such as
and
, it fails open: any tool you forgot to list runs freely.
approves file edits and filesystem operations automatically, which is exactly what a read-only agent must not do.
approves everything in advance. During a bloat review, each of these widens the surface rather than shrinking it.
Skills count toward the surface as well. A skill is a reusable set of instructions kept in a
file inside a
folder. The file opens with frontmatter, a short block of
and
lines between

markers, followed by the instructions themselves. At session start Claude loads only a short listing of each skill's description; the full text loads when the skill is invoked, either by Claude when the description fits the request or by a person typing
. Every skill therefore adds an entry to that listing. The description and the optional
field (trigger phrases or example requests) are cut off together at 1,536 characters to limit context use. If a skill has side effects and a person should decide when it runs, set
in its frontmatter. Claude then won't load it automatically or preload it into subagents, and it runs only when someone types

Exam question

A developer wants to build a code-review agent that must never edit files or run shell commands, even if Claude decides such actions would help, and must not fall back to interactive approval because it runs headless in CI. Which configuration achieves this?
Set allowedTools: ["Read", "Glob", "Grep"] with permissionMode: "dontAsk" so listed tools are approved and everything else is denied outright.
Set disallowedTools: ["Edit", "Write", "Bash"] with permissionMode: "bypassPermissions" so denied tools are blocked while everything else runs freely.
Set allowedTools: ["Read", "Glob", "Grep"] with permissionMode: "default" so unlisted tools fall through to the canUseTool callback for confirmation.
Set permissionMode: "acceptEdits" with no allowedTools entries so file operations are pre-approved but Bash still prompts for confirmation.

Exam question

A lead agent has allowedTools: ["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Bash", "Agent"] for its own broad development work. The team also defines a code-reviewer subagent that should only ever read and search code, never write files or run shell commands, regardless of what the lead agent is permitted to do. How should the subagent be configured to enforce this?
Define the subagent with its own tools: ["Read", "Glob", "Grep"] field in its AgentDefinition, independent of the lead agent's allowedTools.
Rely on the lead agent's allowedTools list, since subagents always inherit a strict subset of whatever tools the lead agent is permitted to use.
Add a CLAUDE.md note describing the reviewer role as read-only, since subagents load the same tool permissions as the invoking session.
Set the lead agent's permissionMode to "plan" whenever the code-reviewer subagent is invoked, which restricts only that subagent's tool access.

Matching the remedy to the source of pressure

Each bloat remedy acts on a different source of pressure, so the diagnosis decides which one to use. Merging, namespacing and scoping change the set of tools an agent has. The context remedies leave the set alone and change where the tokens go. Choose by where your tokens, or your wrong tool calls, are actually coming from.
Source of pressure against the remedy that targets it
Where the pressure comes from
Remedy
What it changes
Overlapping or vaguely bounded tools
Consolidate and namespace
Fewer, clearly separated tools, so selection gets easier
One role holding tools another role needs
Scope with tools, disallowedTools, mcpServers
Each agent loads and can call only its own tools
A large toolset (20+ tools) where most tools aren't needed on a given turn
Tool search
Definitions stay out of context until Claude searches for them
A large but stable toolset sent on many requests
Prompt caching
Repeated definitions cost less; the token count is unchanged
Old tool_result blocks building up in a long conversation
Context editing
Stale results are trimmed from history
Chains of small tool calls that could run as one script
Programmatic tool calling
Intermediate results never enter the conversation
Programmatic tool calling replaces a chain of tool calls with one script. Instead of five round trips of
and

, Claude writes a single block of code that calls all five functions, and Anthropic's code execution sandbox runs it. Only the script's final output returns to the conversation; the intermediate results never enter the history. It fits repetitive chains of small calls that could run as a single batch, and it does nothing for an oversized toolset.
Tool search fixes having too many definitions in context, not having tools that overlap.
Tool search (defer_loading, tool_reference, ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH)

holds back deferred definitions until Claude searches for them. It costs a little latency, one extra turn to look a tool up, and saves a lot of baseline context. It's the right choice when the catalogue is genuinely large and each request needs only a few tools. It does nothing about two tools with blurred boundaries. When a search turns up both of them, Claude faces the same confusing choice as before, so overlap is still fixed by merging and namespacing.

Prompt caching is the other remedy that's easy to misapply. It doesn't reduce the number of tokens in context. It reduces what you pay for them on later requests, so a large fixed toolset gets cheaper but takes up just as much of the window and the attention budget. Use it when the problem is cost. When the problem is selection accuracy or running out of context, merge, scope or defer instead.

The remedies combine without conflict. A sensible order for a high-volume agent is to cache tool definitions from day one, add tool search once the toolset passes roughly 20 tools or baseline context use becomes noticeable, and add context editing when conversations get long enough that early results no longer matter. Merging and scoping come before all of these. A tool you removed costs nothing to defer, cache or trim.
